sort-array-by-increasing-frequency.pattern: Count with a hash map, then sort with a custom comparator (frequency ↑, value ↓)

approaches.name: Count each value by scanning, then sort
approaches.idea: For every element, count its frequency by scanning the whole array; then sort by (frequency ascending, value descending).
steps: For each element, count how many times its value appears by scanning `nums`.
Sort the elements by that frequency ascending, breaking ties by value descending.
Return the sorted array.
approaches.why: Counting by scanning costs O(n) per element; the sort adds O(n log n).

approaches.name: Hash map counts and one sort
approaches.idea: Count every value once in a map, then sort with the two-part key.
steps: Count occurrences with a hash map (or an array offset by 100).
Sort by `count` ascending and, for equal counts, by value descending.
Return the sorted array.
approaches.why: Counting is O(n); the sort dominates.

sort-an-array.pattern: Comparison sorts in O(n log n) (merge sort, heap sort), or counting sort for a small value range

approaches.name: Insertion sort
approaches.idea: Grow a sorted prefix: take the next element and shift larger elements right until its place is found.
steps: For `i` from 1 to n − 1, hold `x = nums[i]`.
Shift every element of the sorted prefix that is greater than `x` one place right.
Put `x` in the gap.
approaches.why: A reversed array needs about n²/2 shifts. Fast on nearly-sorted data, but too slow for the large test.

approaches.name: Merge sort
approaches.idea: Split the array in half, sort each half recursively, and merge the two sorted halves by repeatedly taking the smaller front element.
steps: `sort(lo, hi)`: if the range has one element, it is sorted.
Sort `[lo, mid]` and `[mid + 1, hi]`.
Merge them into a buffer with two pointers, then copy back.
approaches.why: log n levels of splitting, each merging n elements in total. The merge buffer takes O(n). It is stable and never degrades.

approaches.name: Heap sort
approaches.idea: Arrange the array into a max-heap in place, then repeatedly swap the maximum (the root) to the end and restore the heap on the shrinking prefix.
steps: Build a max-heap: sift down every node from `n / 2 − 1` down to 0.
For `end` from n − 1 down to 1: swap `nums[0]` with `nums[end]`, then sift down from 0 within `[0, end)`.
The array is now ascending.
approaches.why: Building the heap is O(n); each of the n extractions sifts down O(log n). It sorts in place with no extra array, but is not stable.

approaches.name: Counting sort (the value range is small)
approaches.idea: Values lie in `[−5·10⁴, 5·10⁴]`, only 10⁵ + 1 possibilities. Count how often each value occurs, then write the values back in order.
steps: Count each value in an array of size `max − min + 1`, indexed by `value − min`.
Walk the counts from smallest value to largest, writing each value as many times as it occurred.
approaches.why: R is the value range (10⁵ + 1 here). Linear when R is small compared to n log n; with a huge range a comparison sort is better.

largest-number.pattern: Custom comparator: put a before b when a + b > b + a (as strings)

approaches.name: Try every ordering
approaches.idea: Generate every permutation of the numbers, join each into a string, and keep the largest (comparing equal-length strings works like comparing numbers).
steps: Turn the numbers into strings.
For every permutation, join the strings; keep the lexicographically largest result (all results have the same length).
If the best result starts with `0`, the answer is `"0"`.
approaches.why: n! orderings, each joined in O(L) where L is the total number of digits. Only feasible for a handful of numbers.

approaches.name: Sort with the concatenation comparator
approaches.idea: For two numbers, whichever order gives the bigger concatenation should come first: `a` before `b` if `a + b > b + a` as strings. This rule is consistent (transitive), so sorting with it gives the best overall order.
steps: Turn the numbers into strings.
Sort with the comparator: `a` before `b` when `a + b > b + a`.
Join the strings. If the first character is `0`, every number was 0: return `"0"`.
approaches.why: O(n log n) comparisons, each building two strings of length up to 2L where L ≤ 10 digits per number.

h-index.pattern: Counting sort into buckets capped at n (or sort descending)

approaches.name: Try every h from n down
approaches.idea: For each candidate `h` from n down to 0, count the papers with at least `h` citations; the first `h` that works is the largest.
steps: For `h` from n down to 1: count papers with `citations >= h`.
If that count is at least `h`, return `h`.
Return 0.
approaches.why: Up to n candidates, each counted over n papers.

approaches.name: Sort descending
approaches.idea: Sorted from most to least cited, the paper at position `i` (0-based) is the (i + 1)-th most cited. h is the number of positions where `citations[i] >= i + 1`.
steps: Sort citations in descending order.
Count leading positions `i` with `citations[i] >= i + 1`; stop at the first that fails.
Return that count.
approaches.why: The sort dominates (aside from its own memory); the scan is O(n).

approaches.name: Bucket counts capped at n
approaches.idea: The h-index is at most n, so any citation count above n can be treated as n. Count papers per citation value `0..n`, then walk from n down, accumulating how many papers have at least that many citations.
steps: Make `bucket[0..n]`; for each paper, increase `bucket[min(c, n)]`.
Walk `h` from n down to 0, adding `bucket[h]` to `papers` (papers with at least h citations).
Return the first `h` with `papers >= h`.
approaches.why: Two linear passes and n + 1 buckets; no comparison sort.

sort-characters-by-frequency.pattern: Count characters, then bucket sort by frequency

approaches.name: Count, then sort the characters by count
approaches.idea: Count each character, sort the distinct characters by count (highest first), and write each one out as many times as it occurs.
steps: Count each character.
Sort the distinct characters by count, descending.
Append each character `count` times and return the string.
approaches.why: Counting is O(n); only the k distinct characters (at most 62 here) are sorted. The output string is O(n).

approaches.name: Bucket sort by count
approaches.idea: A count is between 1 and n, so place each character in the bucket for its count and read the buckets from n down — no comparison sort at all.
steps: Count each character.
Put each distinct character into `bucket[count]`.
For `k` from n down to 1, append every character in `bucket[k]`, `k` times each.
approaches.why: Counting, bucketing and output are all linear in n.

maximum-gap.pattern: Pigeonhole buckets (the max gap is never inside a bucket) or radix sort

approaches.name: Sort and compare neighbours
approaches.idea: Sort the array and take the largest difference between adjacent elements.
steps: If there are fewer than 2 elements, return 0.
Sort the array.
Return the maximum of `nums[i] − nums[i − 1]`.
approaches.why: A comparison sort cannot beat O(n log n), which the problem rules out.

approaches.name: Pigeonhole buckets of width ⌊(max − min) / (n − 1)⌋
approaches.idea: n values spread over `[min, max]` have an average gap of `(max − min) / (n − 1)`, and the largest gap is at least that. With buckets narrower than that, the largest gap can never be inside one bucket — so only each bucket's min and max matter, and the answer is the biggest jump from one non-empty bucket's max to the next one's min.
steps: If fewer than 2 values or `min == max`, return 0.
Bucket width `w = max(1, (max − min) / (n − 1))`; bucket count `(max − min) / w + 1`.
Put each value in bucket `(x − min) / w`, keeping only that bucket's min and max.
Walk the non-empty buckets in order; the answer is the largest `bucketMin − previousBucketMax`.
approaches.why: One pass to bucket and one over at most n buckets. The largest gap is at least ⌈(max − min) / (n − 1)⌉ ≥ w, while two values in the same bucket differ by at most w − 1, so the largest gap always crosses buckets.
